engines.name: Apache Spark
engines.bestFor: Distributed ETL, lakehouse transforms, streaming, large joins
engines.tradeoff: Operational overhead and startup cost for small local jobs

engines.name: DuckDB
engines.scale: Laptop / server; excellent local analytical scans
engines.bestFor: Local analytics, Parquet/JSON querying, embedded data apps
engines.tradeoff: Single-node by design; distribution is external

engines.name: Polars
engines.bestFor: Fast DataFrame workloads with predictable expression API
engines.tradeoff: Smaller ecosystem than pandas/Spark; distributed story is separate

engines.name: Apache DataFusion
engines.bestFor: Building custom SQL/query engines on Arrow
engines.tradeoff: Toolkit rather than turnkey lakehouse platform

engines.name: Trino
engines.bestFor: Federated SQL across heterogeneous data sources
engines.tradeoff: Not a DataFrame library and not a storage layer

engines.name: pandas
engines.bestFor: General-purpose Python data analysis and broad ecosystem compatibility
engines.tradeoff: Memory-bound and often slower on large analytical workloads

formats.name: Apache Parquet
formats.tradeoff: No table-level transactions, snapshots or concurrent metadata management

formats.name: Apache Iceberg
formats.tradeoff: Requires catalog/metadata discipline and engine support

formats.name: Delta Lake
formats.tradeoff: Feature depth can vary by engine/client

formats.name: Apache Hudi
formats.bestFor: Upserts, incremental processing and CDC-heavy lakes
formats.tradeoff: More concepts and tuning knobs than immutable-file approaches

formats.name: DuckLake
formats.bestFor: Simple lakehouse experimentation with DuckDB-style ergonomics
formats.tradeoff: Newer ecosystem; validate production support for required engines

runtimeFrameworks.name: CPython
runtimeFrameworks.coldStart: Low for scripts; framework-dependent for serverless
runtimeFrameworks.concurrency: Threads limited by GIL for CPU-bound Python; multiprocessing/async common
runtimeFrameworks.dataScale: Single-node unless delegated to native/distributed engines
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: Glue, APIs, orchestration, notebooks, ML/data libraries
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: Tight CPU loops without vectorized/native libraries

runtimeFrameworks.name: PySpark
runtimeFrameworks.execution: Python driver/API over Spark JVM engine; Arrow/Pandas UDF paths available
runtimeFrameworks.coldStart: Higher due to Spark session/cluster startup
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: Large joins, ETL, lakehouse pipelines, streaming
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: Small local datasets where cluster startup dominates

runtimeFrameworks.name: Scala + Spark
runtimeFrameworks.execution: Native JVM API with Spark optimizer/runtime
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: Spark-native libraries, JVM-heavy pipelines, lower Python boundary overhead
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: Teams optimized around Python ecosystem and simple SQL/DataFrames

runtimeFrameworks.name: Polars
runtimeFrameworks.dataScale: MB → hundreds of GB depending on memory/streaming
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: Fast local ETL, DataFrames, APIs, analytical preprocessing

runtimeFrameworks.name: DuckDB
runtimeFrameworks.dataScale: MB → TB-scale scans on suitable hardware/object storage
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: Local analytics, Parquet query, embedded SQL, tests

runtimeFrameworks.name: Rust + DataFusion
runtimeFrameworks.dataScale: Single-node by default; embeddable in distributed systems
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: You want turnkey notebooks/ETL instead of engine development

runtimeFrameworks.name: Python serverless function
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: Long-running Spark jobs or large in-memory analytical workloads

runtimeFrameworks.name: Serverless container
runtimeFrameworks.concurrency: Request concurrency per instance + horizontal scaling
runtimeFrameworks.dataScale: Small/medium services; external DB/object store for large data
runtimeFrameworks.bestFor: FastAPI, Polars/DuckDB services, APIs, scheduled container jobs
runtimeFrameworks.avoidWhen: Stateful persistent services without external state

stackLayers.question: Where do the bytes live?
stackLayers.note: Storage is not a query engine or table format. Cost and locality can dominate the layers above it.

stackLayers.question: How are rows/columns encoded?
stackLayers.note: Parquet is persistent columnar storage; Arrow is primarily an in-memory/IPC columnar representation.

stackLayers.question: How do files become a transactional table?
stackLayers.note: Open table formats organize files and metadata; they do not replace the compute engine executing a query.

stackLayers.question: How are tables discovered, secured and governed?
stackLayers.note: A catalog can be independent of the table format or tightly integrated with a platform.

stackLayers.question: Who plans and executes the work?
stackLayers.note: Single-node and distributed engines can read the same Parquet/Iceberg data but have very different startup and scaling economics.

stackLayers.question: How does a developer express transformations?
stackLayers.note: PySpark and Spark SQL can compile to the same Spark engine plan; the API language alone does not determine execution performance.

stackLayers.question: How is desired data state declared and repeated?
stackLayers.note: Orchestration and transformation tools coordinate engines; they are not substitutes for storage or query execution.

stackLayers.question: How is the result used?
stackLayers.note: Serving requirements often determine upstream architecture: interactive BI, batch ML and APIs need different latency/concurrency profiles.
